sections.title: Nodes 0–1 — The problem, and content-addressed snapshots
sections.content:
Where this sits

This is the bottom of the chain. Everything else in Git — branches, merges, remotes, rebases — is built on the storage model introduced here. If this part is solid, most of the rest becomes derivable. If it isn't, the rest becomes memorization.

Every term, from absolute zero

File — a named sequence of bytes stored on a disk. When you save notes.txt, the operating system writes those bytes somewhere and records the name so it can find them again. Two things are being kept: the contents (the bytes) and the name. Hold that distinction — Git separates them in a way most systems don't, and it's the single most confusing thing about Git until you see why.

Directory (also called a folder) — a listing that maps names to files or to other directories. A directory doesn't contain files in a physical sense; it contains entries, each saying "the name notes.txt refers to this data over here." A directory containing directories is how you get nesting.

Version control — the practice of keeping the history of a set of files as it changes, such that you can see what any file looked like at any past point, see what changed between two points, and know who changed it and why. The phrase is literal: you are controlling versions instead of letting them overwrite each other.

Version control system, abbreviated VCS — a program that does the above for you. Git is one. Subversion, Mercurial, and CVS are others.

Repository — the complete set of a project's files plus its entire recorded history, treated as one unit. Often shortened to "repo." When you "clone a repo," you're copying both the files and every version of those files that ever existed. Note the word choice: a repository is a place where things are deposited and kept, which is exactly what it is — a store of every version ever recorded.

Working tree (also working directory, or working copy) — the ordinary files sitting in your project folder that you actually open and edit. It's called a tree because directories nest inside directories, forming a branching structure like a tree's, and it's called working because it's the copy you're currently working on, as opposed to the recorded historical versions which are stored elsewhere and not directly editable. When you open your editor, you are looking at the working tree.

Snapshot — a complete record of the state of every file at one instant. The word comes from photography: a snapshot captures everything in frame at one moment, not just the parts that moved. This is the opposite of recording changes, and the distinction is central to Git.

Diff (short for "difference") — a description of what changed between two versions, usually expressed as lines added and lines removed. If a snapshot is a photograph, a diff is a note saying "compared to the last photo, the vase moved left." Both can describe the same reality; they're just different ways of storing the information.

Hash function — a function that takes any amount of input data and produces a fixed-size output, called the hash or digest. Three properties matter for our purposes. First, it's deterministic: the same input always produces the same output, every time, on every machine, forever. Second, the output is fixed-length regardless of input size — one byte of input and one gigabyte of input both produce the same size result. Third, and this is what makes it useful here, changing even a single bit of input produces a completely different, unpredictable output. There's no partial resemblance; a one-character edit gives you an output that looks entirely unrelated.

SHA-1 — a specific hash function, standing for Secure Hash Algorithm 1, published in 1995. It produces 160 bits of output. Those 160 bits are conventionally written as 40 hexadecimal characters — hexadecimal being base-16, using the digits 0–9 and letters a–f, where each character represents 4 bits, so 160 ÷ 4 = 40 characters. That's why Git identifiers look like e7f9c2a4b8d1... and are always exactly 40 characters long. Git uses SHA-1 for historical reasons; a variant using SHA-256 exists but is essentially unused in practice.

Content-addressed storage — a storage scheme where the name of a stored item is derived from its contents, by hashing them. This is the opposite of the normal arrangement. Normally you choose a name and put whatever you like under it: the name config.txt is a label you picked, and its contents can change while the name stays put. In content-addressed storage you don't choose the name at all — you hand over some bytes, the system hashes them, and the resulting hash is where those bytes live. Change one byte of the content and it's now a different item at a different address. The name and the content are welded together; you cannot change one without changing the other.

Object — in Git's vocabulary, one item stored in the content-addressed store. Git has exactly four kinds, of which three matter right now.

Object store — the collection of all objects, physically living in the directory .git/objects/ inside your repository.

Blob — one of Git's object types, holding the raw contents of a single file. "Blob" is a long-standing computing term meaning Binary Large OBject: an opaque chunk of bytes that the system stores without interpreting. Git does not know or care whether a blob is JavaScript, a photograph, or noise. Crucially, a blob contains only the bytes. Not the filename. Not the path. Not the modification date.

Tree — Git's object type representing one directory. It's a listing of entries, each pairing a name with the hash of what that name refers to — either a blob (a file) or another tree (a subdirectory). This is where filenames actually live. The word overlaps confusingly with "working tree"; a tree object is the stored, immutable representation, while the working tree is the live editable files on disk.

Commit — Git's object type representing one recorded snapshot. It points at exactly one tree, which is the project's root directory at that instant, and carries metadata: who made it, when, and a message saying why. When people say "a commit," they usually mean both the object and the act of creating it.

zlib — a widely used data compression library. Git compresses each object's bytes with zlib before writing them to disk, purely to save space. This is why opening a file in .git/objects/ in a text editor shows unreadable garbage: it's compressed, not corrupted.

Deduplication — storing identical data only once, no matter how many times it appears. Git gets this for free from content-addressing.

The history — why any of this exists

To understand why Git looks the way it does, you have to understand what people were doing before, and specifically what kept failing.

The very first approach — still the default for anyone who hasn't been taught otherwise — is copying the folder. Before making a risky change, you duplicate project into project-backup. This is not stupid; it's the correct instinct, and it does solve the immediate problem of losing the working version. What it fails at is scale. After a month you have project-backup, project-backup-2, project-final, project-final-real, and project-final-USE-THIS-ONE. You've lost the ordering, you've lost the reasons, you've lost the ability to see what differs between any two, and you're storing dozens of near-identical copies of files that mostly never changed. Every one of Git's early design decisions is an attack on one of those five failures.

The first real tools appeared in the early 1970s. SCCS (Source Code Control System, 1972) and then RCS (Revision Control System, 1982) tracked history per file. Each file got its own independent version numbers — notes.txt might be at version 1.7 while main.c was at 1.23. This was a genuine improvement over folder copies, but it had a conceptual flaw that mattered enormously: there was no such thing as a version of the project. If you wanted to recreate how the whole thing looked last Tuesday, you had to know which version of each file was current last Tuesday, and nothing recorded that. The project's state was an unstated combination of per-file states.

CVS (Concurrent Versions System, 1990) layered a multi-user, networked model on top of RCS but inherited the per-file thinking, along with an inability to handle renames sensibly — renaming a file lost its history, because history was attached to the filename.

Subversion, or SVN (2000), was written explicitly to fix CVS, and its key insight is the direct ancestor of Git's model: make the whole repository the versioned unit. An SVN commit produced a single global revision number covering the entire project, so "revision 4,217" unambiguously named a complete state of everything. That's the right idea, and Git kept it.

But SVN was centralized, meaning there was one authoritative server and your local copy was only a working copy — history lived on the server. To commit, to view history, to branch, you needed to reach that server. If it was down or you were offline, you were stuck. And SVN implemented branching as a server-side directory copy, which made branches trivially cheap to create and painful to merge, because the system had only a weak notion of what had already been combined.

Meanwhile the Linux kernel — an enormous project with thousands of contributors — was using BitKeeper, which was distributed: every developer had a complete copy of the entire history locally, with no central authority required. This worked well. The problem was that BitKeeper was proprietary, and in April 2005 its free-for-open-source license was withdrawn after a dispute. The kernel, one of the largest software projects on earth, abruptly had no version control system.

Linus Torvalds wrote the first working version of Git over about ten days that same month. He had three requirements, and every design decision follows from them.

It had to be fast. The kernel is millions of lines across tens of thousands of files, and the workflow involved applying enormous streams of patches. Operations that took minutes were unusable.

It had to be distributed. Every clone must be a complete, self-sufficient repository. No operation should require a network round-trip except explicitly moving data between machines.

It had to make corruption and tampering detectable. This one is the interesting requirement, and it's the one that produced content-addressed storage. In a distributed system, code arrives from many people through many hands. You need to be able to prove that what you received is what was sent, and that history hasn't been quietly altered underneath you.

That third requirement is the direct cause of everything in Node 1. If you name things by the hash of their contents, then verifying integrity requires no extra machinery at all — you re-hash the content and check that it still matches the name it's stored under. Tampering isn't prevented, but it becomes impossible to hide, which is the achievable goal.

The mechanism — traced

Let's follow actual bytes.

You run git init in a folder. Git creates a hidden directory called .git — hidden in the Unix sense that names beginning with a dot aren't shown by default in listings. Inside it, among other things, it creates objects/, an empty directory that will become the object store. That's essentially it. git init is a cheap, local operation that creates a few directories and files; nothing is contacted, nothing is downloaded.

Now you have a file, hello.txt, containing the eleven characters hello world followed by a newline — twelve bytes total. You ask Git to store its contents. Here's what happens, in order.

Step one: build the header. Git does not hash the raw file contents. It first constructs a small prefix: the object's type, a space, the content's length in bytes, and then a null byte — the byte whose value is zero, written as \0, used throughout computing as an end-of-string marker. For our file that prefix is blob 12\0. Git then concatenates the prefix and the content, producing blob 12\0hello world\n.

Why the header? Two reasons. It makes the object self-describing — anything reading the raw bytes back knows immediately what type it is and how long it should be, which is a corruption check in itself. And it means a blob and a tree containing identical bytes hash differently, since their type prefixes differ, avoiding collisions between object types.

Step two: hash it. Git runs SHA-1 over that entire byte sequence, header included, producing 160 bits written as 40 hex characters. For this exact content it's always 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad — on your machine, on mine, in 2005, in 2030. That determinism is the whole foundation.

This is also why running sha1sum hello.txt gives you a different number than Git reports. You hashed twelve bytes; Git hashed twenty. People trip over this constantly.

Step three: compress. Git runs the whole thing — header and content together — through zlib deflate. Space saving, nothing conceptual.

Step four: write it. The compressed bytes go to a path built from the hash: the first two characters become a directory name, the remaining thirty-eight become the filename. Our object lands at .git/objects/3b/18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad.

Why split it? Purely practical. Some filesystems degrade badly when a single directory holds hundreds of thousands of entries. Splitting on the first two hex characters gives 256 possible subdirectories (16 × 16), spreading objects roughly evenly and keeping each directory a couple of hundred times smaller. It's a small engineering accommodation, not a conceptual feature.

Now — the two payoffs.

Deduplication falls out automatically. Suppose you record a snapshot of a thousand files, then change three and record another. For each unchanged file, Git computes its hash, gets the same 40 characters as before, and finds that path already exists. Nothing is written. Only the three changed files produce new objects. So although conceptually every commit references a complete snapshot of all thousand files, physically the second snapshot cost three new objects. This is the resolution of the paradox that trips people up — "Git stores full snapshots" and "Git repositories aren't enormous" are both true, and content-addressing is why.

Integrity falls out automatically. Any object's name is a claim about its contents. Re-hash the contents; if the result doesn't match the name, the object is corrupt or altered. git fsck does exactly this across the entire store.

Now the filename problem. Blobs hold contents only. So where does hello.txt live? In a tree object. A tree is a list of entries, each with four parts: a mode (a number encoding what kind of entry it is — 100644 for an ordinary file, 100755 for an executable one, 40000 for a subdirectory), the type, the hash of the thing it points to, and the name. Sorted by name.

Two consequences worth sitting with.

Renaming a file creates no new blob. The contents didn't change, so the hash didn't change, so the blob is untouched. What changes is the tree — a new tree object with a different name in one entry, pointing at the very same blob. Git therefore doesn't really "track renames" as an event; it stores states and infers renames afterward by noticing that a blob disappeared from one path and an identical one appeared at another. This is why Git handles renames gracefully where CVS couldn't: history was never attached to filenames in the first place.

Two files with identical contents share one blob. Copy hello.txt to greeting.txt and commit. One blob, two tree entries. The object store has no idea these are "two files" — it holds one piece of content that two names happen to refer to.

And an empty directory cannot be represented. A tree is a list of entries. An empty directory has no entries, so there's nothing to write, and no tree can encode "there is a directory here containing nothing." Git isn't refusing to support this; the data model has no expression for it. Hence the universal convention of dropping a placeholder file, usually named .gitkeep, inside directories that need to exist while empty. The name is convention only — Git attaches no meaning to it.

Finally, the third object type: the commit. It's a small text object that names one tree — the root directory of the whole project at that instant — plus author and committer identities with timestamps, and your message. That single tree hash transitively covers everything: the root tree names subtrees by hash, those name blobs by hash, and each hash is derived from its contents. So one 40-character commit identifier is, in effect, a fingerprint of the project's complete state.

That property is what Node 2 builds on.

What an interviewer does with this

"What does a commit actually contain?" A strong answer names the parts — a pointer to one tree, parent pointers, author and committer with timestamps, a message — and then makes the snapshot-versus-diff point explicitly, because that's the real thing being probed. A weak answer says "the changes you made," which is the single most common misconception and reveals that the model isn't there.

"If Git stores full snapshots, why aren't repositories huge?" The answer is content-addressing producing automatic deduplication: unchanged files hash to identifiers that already exist in the store, so nothing new is written for them. Being able to say "only the three files that changed produced new objects" is the difference between having the model and repeating a slogan. There's a second mechanism, packfiles, that compresses further — that's Node 12, and mentioning that it exists without overclaiming is a good look.

"Why is Git's history considered tamper-evident?" Because an object's name is derived from its contents, so altering contents invalidates the name. The full version of this answer needs Node 2's parent chain to be complete; at this level, being precise about the object-level property is enough.

"Why does Git handle renames well when older systems didn't?" Because filenames live in trees, not in blobs, so history was never keyed to a filename. A rename is a new tree pointing at an unchanged blob. Older per-file systems attached history to the filename itself, so renaming severed it.
